'Fahrenheit 451' film in the works at HBO
I think that they've tried this before but the issue was that E-books undermined the premise of the movie. Although that said you could argue that it was never really about the technology.

It wasn't just books, but any form of writing. The 1966 film had absolutely no text whatsoever, except for on the illegal books. Even the opening credits were spoken and not presented as text. With this in mind, you could envision a world where all writing is banned, even with technology present.
This is entirely correct. Much like 1984, the central theme of the story was controlling thought and the spread of ideas. Books were seen as the medium of choice for political dissidents.

I can't remember if this was the case or not in the book but if it was then it creates the a rather massive plot hole in how the main character was able to read if all forms of text had been banned. Sure you could argue that this is a relatively simple skill to acquire but I imagine that if you were to give someone a book that had absolutely no concept of reading it would be the equivalent of giving them a book written in a foreign language. That is while it's possible given enough time someone could translate it enough to a level to read it by themselves, it just doesn't seem creditable.

If memory serves books were "banned" but they still allowed text in the form of instruction manuals, advertising etc. The reason for the quotation marks around banned is that I think in the book it was mentioned that they never actually technically banned books but rather this culture of burning books was more a part of a theater that had grown up as a means to alleviate the anxiety of the society of the modern world in it's relationship to the past. Actually it's depressing how close the guy got to the current world, now I think about it.

That's a really good point. I hadn't thought of asking how could he read.

It makes sense that what they were really after was the expression of thought and ideas, conveyed through books. It wasn't the concept of text they were after.

And yeah, the anxiety of the modern world and the way we view the past is exactly the same reason certain books and ideas are considered problematic by some today. Our societal values change over time, for better or worse. When we view and judge old works from a purely contemporary perspective, we might see them negatively, and worry it could affect our current world views. Of course, this is exactly what we are starting to see in many schools and universities, where a radical fringe is suppressing and editing books that conflict with our modern sensibilities. That's why Fahrenheit 451 has returned to the spotlight so much in recent years, just like how 1984 gained so much attention after the Snowden leaks.
